system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2153-11-18 20:16:00 to 2153-11-19 17:44:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease status post kidney transplant, and severe peripheral vascular disease was admitted for severe left leg pain due to necrotic infection and gangrene. He underwent a two-stage left below-knee amputation: first a guillotine amputation followed by re-amputation with closure. He received blood transfusions preoperatively to support hemoglobin levels and was treated with intravenous vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole for infection, later transitioning to oral antibiotics. Pain was managed with a Dilaudid PCA initially, then oral hydromorphone, acetaminophen, and pregabalin. The nephrology team optimized tacrolimus and blood pressure medications to protect his transplant. The wound healed well, and he was discharged to extended care with plans for rehabilitation and outpatient follow-up. His right hand showed dry gangrene of multiple digits, but no acute intervention was needed.
problems: Atherosclerosis of native arteries of extremities with gangrene, left leg
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic chronic kidney disease
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic peripheral angiopathy with gangrene

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You came in tonight because of some cough and nausea, but we also noticed your oxygen levels dropped while you were sleeping. Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had a bit of a cough and felt kind of sick, but nothing too bad. I didn’t think I needed to come in, but they said my blood pressure was high and my oxygen was low when I was asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your oxygen dipped below normal while you were resting, which is concerning. You mentioned you have sleep apnea—have you been using your CPAP machine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I tried it years ago, but it made me uncomfortable. I haven’t used it since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that might explain the low oxygen. A recent sleep study suggested you may have complex sleep apnea, where CPAP can sometimes make breathing pauses worse. The sleep specialist recommends trying oxygen at night instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oxygen? Like a nasal cannula? I’ve used that before. I think I can handle that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’re arranging for home oxygen—3 liters per minute at night. It’ll be delivered to your house tomorrow before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than the CPAP mask. Will I need it forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need to follow up with another supervised sleep study as an outpatient to be sure. For now, this should help keep your oxygen levels stable at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your kidney function and transplant. Everything looks stable—your creatinine is about the same as usual, and your tacrolimus level is in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been taking my meds regularly, except yesterday I forgot because I was nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We gave you your usual medications here, including your insulin, blood pressure pills, and tacrolimus. Your blood pressure has come down nicely since you got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high BP on and off. My nephrologist was thinking about adding another med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a serum renin level today to help evaluate the cause. Your outpatient team will review that and decide if any changes are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look stable. Your oxygen was 95% on room air while awake, and your kidney and diabetes markers haven’t changed much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you later today. Your back pain is better with the lidocaine patch and Tylenol, and your cough is improving. The main thing is setting up your nighttime oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I want to make sure I’m not missing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on all your usual medications. We’ve updated your list—nothing new except the oxygen at night. A nurse will go over everything with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot and hand? They’ve been dry and cold, but no new pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your amputation sites are healing well, and your circulation is stable for now. Continue with your aspirin and statin, and keep following up with your vascular doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The oxygen supplier confirmed delivery to your home this afternoon. Once it arrives, start using it at night as prescribed—3 liters via nasal cannula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll see my sleep doctor soon for the next test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll schedule a supervised sleep study as an outpatient. Also, your nephrologist will follow up on the renin test and your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Everything’s ready for discharge. You’re doing well—oxygen stable, no fever, and you’re able to walk independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’m glad it wasn’t anything more serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just remember to use the oxygen at night, take your meds, and keep your follow-up appointments. Call if you have any trouble breathing or new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease status post kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease with prior amputations, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for cough, nausea, and nocturnal hypoxia. His blood pressure was elevated on presentation but improved with medication. He was found to have oxygen desaturation during sleep, consistent with his known sleep apnea, which he had not been treating due to CPAP discomfort. A plan was made with the sleep team to initiate nocturnal home oxygen at 3 liters per minute instead of PAP therapy, given concern for complex sleep apnea. His kidney function remained stable, tacrolimus levels were therapeutic, and his other chronic conditions were managed without change. He was discharged home the following day with arranged oxygen delivery and plans for outpatient follow-up with sleep and nephrology specialists.
